🐛 Describe the bug
AMP implementation for torch.cat seems to be broken for CPU.
I noticed with gdb that with PyTorch 1.12, at::native::to is called for the second tensor with the following snippet of code, but not with PyTorch 1.13 release branch, or with the master branch:
import torch
with torch.cpu.amp.autocast(cache_enabled=False, dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    a = torch.rand(24, 128, 128)
    b = torch.rand(24, 128, 128, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    c = torch.cat([a, b], 0)
I strongly suspect that this is an AMP issue (probably introduced by #73350, as it doesn't happen before that PR's commit).
Also, when I run the following script (with JIT AMP disabled, tracing a function that calls torch.cat with eager-mode AMP),
I see an aten::to node with PyTorch 1.12 but not PyTorch 1.13 release branch / master branch.
import torch
torch._C._jit_set_autocast_mode(False)

def printTracedModel(model, input):
   with torch.no_grad(), torch.cpu.amp.autocast(cache_enabled=False, dtype=torch.bfloat16):
       traced = torch.jit.trace(model, input)
       fwd_graph = traced.graph_for(*input)
       print(fwd_graph)

def test_cat_check_type_promotion():
   def cat_along_dim(d):
       def forward_cat(*inputs):
           return torch.cat(inputs, d)
       return forward_cat

   x = torch.rand(24, 128, 128)
   y = torch.rand(24, 128, 128, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
   printTracedModel(cat_along_dim(0), [x, y])

if __name__ == '__main__':
   test_cat_check_type_promotion()
Versions
Master branch & Release 1.13 branch.
Release 1.12 is fine, so this is a regression (if this issue really exists)
To quickly verify, one can use:

        position_ids = torch.arange(input_ids.size(1), dtype=torch.long).unsqueeze(0)
        position_ids = position_ids.expand(input_ids.size())  # Issue here
        # position_ids = position_ids.repeat(input_ids.size(0), 1)  # Workaround

torch.onnx.export(
    TestModel(),
    torch.ones(1, 512),
    'tmp.onnx',
    input_names=['input_ids'],
    output_names=['output'],
    dynamic_axes={
        'input_ids': {0: 'batch_size', 1: 'sequence_length'},

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
The module hierarchy in PyTorch networks is saved in nn.module.named_modules().  This function provides a unique name that maps to each module object in the network.  However, when torch.fx.symbolic_trace() is run on a network, the module hierarchy is lost in the resulting torch.fx.GraphModule.    The unique module names effectively describe the network architecture.  Here's an example name from Hugging Face stable diffusion
text_model.encoder.layers.0.self_attn.mul . torchFX would convert this name to just mul_1 .   From the HF example, just by looking at the module name we can tell the op is part of the encoder from the 0th layer in the self_attn block.  Whereas with the name mul_1 we can't tell what part of the network this operator belongs to.
In torch.fx the network graph is stored in the GraphModule.graph.nodes class.  However, the nodes are just a flat listing of all the operators in the network, they don't include any references to the modules which defined the nodes.  The PyTorch ONNX exporter was recently updated to include the module information in the operator unique names.  This feature request is proposing to do the same for torch.FX.
Alternatives
Live with the current default node names and refer directly to the network source code to try and understand the network architecture.
Additional context
Here's an example of what the unique operator (graph.node) names should look like.  Just by viewing the graph or the listing from graph.graph you can understand the network architecture which is much easier to work with than inspecting the network source code.

🐛 Describe the bug
For a model fn(x, y) -> max(x, y) where x is double and y is float, PyTorch will implicitly promote the output to double. When exporting such a model to ONNX, the implicit casting is not considered. In ONNX's standard, Max or similar operators must take inputs whose types are the same, therefore, such models are invalid and ONNXRuntime will abort when accepting them.
Unfortunately, the ONNX checker also has a bug here that lets this specific case escape: onnx/onnx#4619
To reproduce:
import torch
from io import BytesIO
import onnx


class M(torch.nn.Module):
    @torch.no_grad()
    def forward(self, x, y):
        return torch.max(x, y)


inputs = (
    torch.randn((2, 2, 1, 1), dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn((), dtype=torch.float32),
)
f = BytesIO()
torch.onnx.export(M(), inputs, f, opset_version=13)

onnx_model = onnx.load_from_string(f.getvalue())
onnx.checker.check_model(onnx_model, full_check=True)
assert M()(*inputs).dtype == torch.float64
print(onnx.helper.printable_graph(onnx_model.graph))
Expected output:
"""
graph torch_jit (
  %onnx::Max_0[DOUBLE, 2x2x1x1]
  %onnx::Max_1[FLOAT, scalar]
) {
  %2 = Max(%onnx::Max_0, %onnx::Max_1)
  return %2
}
"""
This graph is invalid because Max takes different types of inputs.
Another interesting fact is that this seems only happens for Max. If we use Min/Add/etc., the output ONNX model correctly produces the implicit casting node:
"""
graph torch_jit (
  %onnx::Min_0[DOUBLE, 2x2x1x1]
  %onnx::Cast_1[FLOAT, scalar]
) {
  %/Cast_output_0 = Cast[to = 11](%onnx::Cast_1)
  %3 = Min(%onnx::Min_0, %/Cast_output_0)
  return %3
}
"""

        #return [x, x]

model.register_full_backward_hook(print_hook)
y = model(x)['x']
loss = (y**2).sum()

print('backward started')
loss.backward()
print('backward complete')

backward started
backward complete

backward started
hook triggered on TestModule(

backward complete

It is recommended to set a large seed, i.e. a number that has a good balance of 0 and 1 bits. Avoid having many 0 bits in the seed.

This is not accurate and seems to be cause by a confusion between the generator state and seed. It's important that the state has a good balance of 0 and 1 bits, but this is handled by the initialization sequence. Early (pre-2002) versions of mt19937 had poor initialization routines, but that's been fixed for 20 years and was never an issue in PyTorch.
Note that the docs for mt19937 explicitly mention zero as a valid seed: "init_genrand(seed) initializes the state vector by using one unsigned 32-bit integer 'seed', which may be zero."
http://www.math.sci.hiroshima-u.ac.jp/m-mat/MT/MT2002/CODES/readme-mt.txt
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
The docs should say that any 32-bit integer is a valid seed. Alternatively, we can refer the reader to https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.08203.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.nn.parameter import Parameter
from apex.contrib.layer_norm.layer_norm import FastLayerNorm
import torchdynamo

tensor_dtype = torch.float16

class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(Net, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(768, 768, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(768, 2048, bias=False)
        self.fast_layer_norm = FastLayerNorm(768)
        self.bias = Parameter(torch.rand(768))

    def forward(self, x, residuals):
        out      = self.fc1(x)
        out      = out + self.bias
        out      = F.dropout(out, p=0.1, training=True)
        ln_input = out + residuals
        ln_out = self.fast_layer_norm(ln_input)
        out1     = self.fc2(ln_out)
        return out1

device = torch.device("cuda:0" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

net = Net()
net.cuda()
net = net.half()

input_shapes    = [(512, 64, 768),
                   (512, 64, 768)]

    for tensor in input_tensors:

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
There are situations such as ablation studies, custom fusion implementations and debugging that would benefit from disabling PyTorch fusion during quantization. It does not appear that this is currently possible without writing your own _prepare_fx function.
I also think this is a reasonable request because fusion is currently supported separately via fuse_fx, but during FX quantization fusion always occurs. If the two operations are implemented separately, I don't see why the user shouldn't be able to perform them separately.
Alternatives
With the addition of a prepare_custom_config it appears the right way to do this would be to add a second fuse_custom_config argument to prepare_fx. Currently the FuseCustomConfig object is default-constructed and cannot be modified by the user.
Another option would be to just add a flag like fuse to prepare_fx and then only call _fuse_fx if this flag is set.

🐛 Describe the bug
Describe the bug
Exported ONNX graphs retain the names for zero dimensional and one dimensional parameters, but rename any two or more dimensional parameters. This makes writing scripts for later graph manipulation much more tedious and prone to breaking.
Note, I originally created this issue in the NVIDIA/NeMo repository, as that is the codebase I was using when I ran into the issue. They stated that this behavior is not due to their implementation, but due to PyTorch internals, which is why I'm here. I did my best to find the files in PyTorch's implementation responsible for this, but couldn't figure it out, and would love help finding where this is occurring and why.
Steps/Code to reproduce bug
from nemo.collections.nlp.models.machine_translation import MTEncDecModel

model = MTEncDecModel.from_pretrained('nmt_en_de_transformer12x2')
model.decoder.export('pretrained_decoder.onnx')
Open pretrained_decoder.onnx in Netron or some other ONNX graph visualizer. Find and compare the inputs to the nodes MatMul_106 and Add_107.

Add_107 takes 1D tensors as input, and has preserved the name of the parameters from the NeMo model. Its first input is _decoder.layers.0.first_sub_layer.query_net.bias.
MatMul_106 requires a 2D tensor as input, and has renamed the parameter from the NeMo model from the quite helpful _decoder.layers.0.first_sub_layer.query_net.weight to the generic onnx::MatMul_636.

Some extra details that I've realized:

This doesn't occur with all 2D parameters: _embedding.token_embedding.weight is preserved, for instance, despite being a (32000, 1024) tensor. It does occur to most, however.
This might be caused by constant folding: When I call the export function with do_constant_folding=False, the parameters are not renamed (although the graph is different, now, of course, because constants were not folded in)

Expected behavior
I'd love for it to respect the names of all parameters, which would create a predictable and reliable ONNX graph that can then be further post-processed as needed. I'd simultaneously love to be able to use constant folding. At the very least, I'd love to understand why this happens and if it's necessary for some reason.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Hi,
I'm working on the R bindings for LibTorch. The R language has a very lazy garbage collector, thus memory is only released to the OS when R needs more memory, LibTorch Tensors are exposed as pointer like R objects, so R is not aware of the memory they use and thus almost never calls GC. In the CUDA case we have fixed this using a callback that just calls the R garbage collector when an allocation fails.
In v1.12.1 LibTorch has support for MPS allocator callbacks:

  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/mps/MPSAllocator.mm
    
    
         Line 132
      in
      664058f
    
  
  
    

        
          
           trigger_memory_callbacks(buffer_block, IMpsAllocatorCallback::EventType::FREED); 
        
    
  


Although they can't really be used for that purpose (explanation below), but callbacks are no longer called since a recent PR (#86119).
Problems with v1.12.1 callbacks implementation:

They are only called late - ie. when releasing cached blocks to the OS, and this might not happen since macOS does a lot of swapping, so allocations before that never fail. It would be nice to call them by looking at memory pressure or something similar.
They can't free memory. If you try to release MPSAllocator allocated memory, you inevitably call Free which acquires the same mutex that Malloc is using, thus deadlocking.

Alternatives
I wonder if you would be open to a PR that:

Re-adds support for the memory callbacks.
Fixes the issues cited above so they can work for freeing memory.

I have a patch that we are using in our custom builds of LibTorch for arm macs here.
It uses a recursive mutex to fix 2. And just calls trigger_callbacks earlier than what happens in v1.12.1 to fix 1.
Additional context
Thank you very much!

🐛 Describe the bug
Issue:
With torch.float16 precision, tensor product @ from several released pytorch versions produce different output results when batch size is changed. (nn.Linear is also affected)
This bug may be serious in networks with multiple stacked linear layers like Transformers, since errors could be accumlated through layers. It seems like this bug existed from version 1.10 to 1.14, and as far as I know many new models from various work were trained on these releases.
How to reproduce?
import torch
import random
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast

seed = 1234
dtype = torch.float16

random.seed(seed)
torch.manual_seed(seed)
torch.cuda.manual_seed(seed)
torch.cuda.set_device(0)
torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False

net = nn.Linear(768, 768).to('cuda:0', dtype=dtype)
net.eval()

y = torch.randn(N, 768).to('cuda:0', dtype=dtype)
